vocabulary.term: よろしくお願いします
vocabulary.translation: Please treat me well / nice to meet you

grammar.title: The topic particle は (wa)
grammar.explanation: は marks the topic of the sentence and is pronounced 'wa' (not 'ha') in this role. '私は学生です' (Watashi wa gakusei desu) = 'As for me, I am a student.' The verb/state comes at the end, after です (desu).

examples.text: はじめまして。私はアナです。よろしくお願いします。
examples.translation: Nice to meet you. I'm Ana. Please treat me well.

content.tip: Say your self-introduction (name + one fact) out loud until it's automatic — it's used constantly in Japan.

grammar.title: Counters change with the object
grammar.explanation: Japanese uses different counting words depending on what's being counted: 一つ (hitotsu, generic objects), 一人 (hitori, people), 一本 (ippon, long thin objects). There's no single universal 'one' like English.

examples.text: りんごを二つください。

content.tip: Learn counters in small groups tied to real objects you actually count often — don't try to learn all of them at once.

grammar.title: 〜をください for requests
grammar.explanation: Attach を (object marker) + ください to the thing you want: 'コーヒーをください' (Please give me coffee). It's simple, polite, and used constantly when ordering.

examples.text: すみません、コーヒーをください。

content.tip: Practice ordering your actual daily drink using 〜をください before you next order it for real.

grammar.title: Polite past tense: ました / でした
grammar.explanation: Polite verbs ending in ます become past by swapping to ました: 行きます → 行きました. Polite い-adjectives drop い and add かった + です: 楽しい → 楽しかったです.

examples.text: 昨日、公園に行きました。楽しかったです。
examples.translation: Yesterday I went to the park. It was fun.

content.tip: Narrate your actual day in three simple past-tense sentences each evening.
